title: Precision CRISPR Guide RNA Design for Differentially Expressed Genes in COVID-19
text:
Preface
This report presents our group project for IFN646 Biomedical Data Science at Queensland University of Technology. It connects three stages of a biomedical data analysis: identifying changes in gene expression, selecting CRISPR guide RNAs, and assessing how human genetic variation may affect those guides.
The project uses real biomedical data within a teaching scenario. Its working hypothesis is that regulating genes affected by COVID-19 could support recovery. This hypothesis provides a reason for the analysis; the project does not test whether the proposed guides improve clinical outcomes.
The report follows the decisions from the RNA-seq analysis to the evaluation of OAS2 and the selected guides 200forw and 248forw. Each task explains the approach, presents the findings, and discusses what the results support. The final chapters bring these findings together and document how to reproduce the analysis.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
This report presents a three-stage analysis of biomedical data. The project explores how differential-expression results can support CRISPR guide design in a teaching scenario about COVID-19.
The project uses three statements to frame the analysis:

COVID-19 patients suffer from a deregulation in gene expression.
CRISPR can be used to regulate the expression of specific genes of interest.
Restoring the expression of selected genes could improve recovery. This is the fictional working hypothesis used for the project.

The analysis addresses three tasks. It does not test whether the proposed guides improve recovery:

Differential Expression Analysis: Using raw RNA-seq counts and agreement between two tools to identify genes with different expression in SARS and mock samples.
CRISPR Guide RNA (gRNA) Design: Selecting guides in the first exon of a consensus gene, choosing CRISPRi or CRISPRa based on the expression change, and comparing predicted efficiency and specificity.
Genomic Variation Assessment: Using individual variant information to reassess guide suitability and possible off-target recognition. For the selected CRISPRi strategy, unintended gene regulation is the relevant concern.

title: 2  Task 1: Differential Expression Analysis
text:
2.1 Tool Selection and Preprocessing
An RNA-seq differential-expression analysis compared the SARS condition with the mock control. The six count columns represent two donors, each with one sample in the Rem, SARS and mock conditions at 5 days after infection. Metadata was extracted from names such as S_2_SARS_5dpi_S70003 using the pattern S_{donor}_{condition}_{time}_{sample_id}. All six samples were included in the models, but the reported contrast tests SARS against mock, not Rem against mock.
The count matrix contained 60,683 genes. Removing 27,356 genes with zero counts in all six samples left 33,327 genes before tool-specific filtering. This follows the gene-level filtering step discussed in Lecture 4: genes without counts cannot provide evidence of an expression change.
Both tools used the design ~ donor + condition. This accounts for differences between donors while estimating the condition effect. The pairing of the samples supports this design, and the PCA provides a visual check of donor-related variation (Figure 2.1).
PC1 explains 53% of the variation and separates the two donor groups. Donor 2 samples cluster together, while donor 3 samples are more spread out. This supports including donor in the model. As discussed in Lecture 4, PCA helps identify sample structure; it does not prove which factor causes all variation. With only two donors, the expression results remain evidence for this experiment rather than a general estimate for all COVID-19 patients.
DESeq2 (Love, Huber, and Anders 2014) and edgeR (Robinson, McCarthy, and Smyth 2009) were selected because both model RNA-seq counts with a negative binomial distribution. This allows the variance to be larger than the mean, as often occurs in these data. Lecture 4 also presents these tools as suitable choices, while noting that no method performs best in every dataset. Their different normalisation, filtering and dispersion procedures allow us to check whether a result depends on one analysis method. Data preparation used tidyverse (Wickham et al. 2019).
Data preprocessing was tailored to the requirements of each tool:
Show analysis code
design_matrix <- model.matrix(
  design,
  data = col_data
)

y <- DGEList(counts = counts_data, sample = col_data)
keep <- filterByExpr(y, design = design_matrix)
y <- y[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE]
y <- calcNormFactors(y)

title: 2  Task 1: Differential Expression Analysis
text:
For DESeq2: Counts were normalised with the median-of-ratios method. During results generation, independent filtering was used to exclude low-information genes from multiple-testing adjustment. Genes without an adjusted p-value were excluded from the significant list.
For edgeR: filterByExpr removed genes with insufficient expression for the design. Library sizes were then recalculated and TMM normalisation was applied. Both normalisation methods account for differences in sequencing depth and RNA composition; the models use counts rather than TPM or FPKM.

title: 2  Task 1: Differential Expression Analysis
section: 2.2 Quality Control and Individual Tool Results
text:
2.2 Quality Control and Individual Tool Results
The dispersion plots show how both tools estimate variation between samples (Figure 2.2 and Figure 2.3). Low-count genes show a wider spread of estimates, while the fitted trends decline as expression increases.
For DESeq2, the black points are gene-wise dispersion estimates, the red line is the fitted trend and the blue points are the final estimates after shrinkage. The edgeR plot shows the biological coefficient of variation, the square root of dispersion, with gene-specific points and common and trend estimates. Sharing information across genes helps estimate variation with few replicates. These plots are useful checks, but they do not prove that every gene fits the model or that all significant results are true positives.








Figure 2.2: Dispersion Estimates (DESeq2)













Figure 2.3: Biological Coefficient of Variation (edgeR)





Both models tested the SARS condition against mock while accounting for donor. DESeq2 used its default Wald test, and edgeR used a GLM likelihood ratio test. Positive log2 fold changes indicate higher expression in SARS; negative values indicate lower expression.


Show analysis code
#DESeq2 results
res_deseq <- results(
  dds,
  contrast = c(
    "condition",
    "SARS",
    "mock"
  ),
  alpha = 0.05
)

#EdgeR results
fit_edger <- glmFit(y_dispersion, design_matrix)

lrt <- glmLRT(
  fit_edger,
  coef = "conditionSARS"
)



DESeq2 results were filtered using a Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value (padj) < 0.05.
edgeR results were filtered using a Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05. As discussed in Lecture 4, this addresses the many gene-level tests rather than applying an unadjusted p-value threshold.



Show analysis code
sig_deseq <- deseq_results |>
  filter(
    padj < 0.05
  )

sig_edger <- edger_results |>
  filter(
    FDR < 0.05
  )

print(paste0("Significant genes: ", nrow(sig_deseq), " found by DESeq2 and ", nrow(sig_edger), " found by EdgeR"))


[1] "Significant genes: 68 found by DESeq2 and 7 found by EdgeR"


DESeq2 identified 68 significant genes, while edgeR identified 7. The lists differ even though both use a 0.05 adjusted threshold. Their filtering, normalisation, dispersion estimates and statistical tests differ, and these can affect which genes pass the threshold. The counts alone do not show that one method is more accurate. The consensus below checks which results remain significant under both methods.

title: 2  Task 1: Differential Expression Analysis
text:
2.3 Consensus Strategy
The significant lists were joined by gene identifier, retaining only genes significant in both tools. This intersection gives priority to results supported by both methods. It is conservative: a real expression change may be excluded if only one tool detects it. The tools also use the same samples, so their agreement is a sensitivity check rather than independent experimental confirmation.
A second filter required the DESeq2 log2 fold change and edgeR logFC to have the same sign. This avoids selecting a gene when the tools disagree on whether expression increased or decreased. The consensus table (Table 2.1) reports gene identifiers, annotations, effect sizes and adjusted significance values, and provides the candidates for Task 2.


Show analysis code
consensus_table <- sig_deseq |>
  select(
    gene_id,
    fold_change_deseq = log2FoldChange,
    adj_p_value_deseq = padj
  ) |>
  inner_join(
    sig_edger |>
      select(gene_id, fold_change_edger = logFC, adj_p_value_edger = FDR),
    by = "gene_id"
  ) |> 
  filter(sign(fold_change_deseq) == sign(fold_change_edger)) |> 
  left_join(
    raw_counts_data |> 
      select(1:6),
    by = join_by(gene_id)
  ) |> 
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ as.character(signif(.x, 3))))

The consensus contains six genes: OAS2, GPRASP1, AC026801.2, IFI27, SERPINB2 and CXCL11. Five are upregulated; SERPINB2 is downregulated. This corresponds to 6 of the 7 edgeR hits and 6 of the 68 DESeq2 hits. The final rule did not retain 62 DESeq2 hits and 1 edgeR hit.
OAS2, GPRASP1 and AC026801.2 have the largest positive log2 fold changes, close to 10 or higher. IFI27 and CXCL11 show smaller positive changes, while SERPINB2 has similar negative estimates in both tools (-1.69 and -1.67). The annotation identifies AC026801.2 as a long non-coding RNA and the other five as protein-coding genes. Thus, the consensus includes both increased and decreased expression and more than one gene type.
Large effect estimates need care. GPRASP1 and AC026801.2 have zero counts in both mock samples, and OAS2 has only 0 and 2. The reported fold changes are model estimates without additional fold-change shrinkage. Low baseline expression and the small number of donors limit how precisely these large changes can be interpreted.
OAS2 was selected for Task 2 because both methods support increased expression and its role in the antiviral OAS pathway is described in the available literature (Merold et al. 2025). The largest fold change alone would not be enough to justify this choice. These results identify candidates for the project; they do not show that reducing any of these genes would improve recovery.

title: 3  Task 2: gRNA design for OAS2
text:
3.1 Target gene selection
Task 1 identified six genes that were significant in both DESeq2 and edgeR. Both methods also agreed on the direction of the expression change. The six consensus genes are shown in Table 2.1.
For Task 2, we selected OAS2 (ENSG00000111335). OAS2 showed a strong increase in expression in the SARS condition with both differential-expression methods. It also has a clear role in the human antiviral response. OAS2 is part of the interferon-induced OAS pathway and contributes to activation of RNase L after viral double-stranded RNA is detected (Merold et al. 2025). OAS family genes have also been linked to severe COVID-19 and COVID-19-related heart failure (Gao et al. 2023; Hernandez-Ramirez et al. 2026).
The Task 1 result for OAS2 is summarised in Table 3.1.

OAS2 had a DESeq2 log2 fold change of 9.90 and an edgeR logFC of 10.30, with adjusted values of 9.69e-10 and 0.000169, respectively. Both methods support increased expression in SARS compared with mock. The table’s “Fold change” column contains log2 values, not expression ratios. The low mock counts and two-donor design limit the interpretation of the size of this change.

title: 3  Task 2: gRNA design for OAS2
text:
3.2 Choice of CRISPR strategy
The project hypothesis is that restoring deregulated gene expression may improve recovery. Because OAS2 was upregulated, we selected CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) to reduce transcription. CRISPRi uses catalytically inactive Cas9 with a repressor such as KRAB (Jensen et al. 2021). This follows the direction-based choice in the project brief. OAS2 also has an antiviral role, so increased expression does not by itself show that repression would be beneficial (Merold et al. 2025).
The project asks for guides within the first exon. We therefore used the first exon of the OAS2 MANE Select transcript. This meets the project’s target-region requirement; it does not establish that these sites give the strongest CRISPRi repression.

title: 3  Task 2: gRNA design for OAS2
text:
3.3 OAS2 transcript selection
OAS2 was inspected in Ensembl using the human GRCh38.p14 reference assembly. The gene is located on chromosome 12 and is on the forward strand.
The MANE Select transcript ENST00000392583.7 was selected. MANE provides a representative transcript that is matched between NCBI and EMBL-EBI (Morales et al. 2022).

title: 3  Task 2: gRNA design for OAS2
text:
3.5 Guide design with CRISPOR
Several guide-design tools are available, including SSC, E-CRISP, CHOPCHOP and CRISPOR (Li et al. 2023; Cui et al. 2018). Lecture 6 separates guide assessment into efficiency at the intended site and specificity against other sites. We selected CRISPOR because it reports both types of prediction and provides downloadable off-target sequences and genomic locations for Task 3 (Concordet and Haeussler 2018).
The CRISPOR analysis used the following settings:

Reference genome: Homo sapiens GRCh38/hg38
Target sequence: first exon of OAS2 (ENSE00002421397.2)
Nuclease: SpCas9
PAM: NGG
Guide length: 20 bp







Figure 3.3: CRISPOR input settings used for the OAS2 first exon. The human GRCh38/hg38 reference genome and the 20bp-NGG SpCas9 PAM setting were selected.



After submitting the sequence, CRISPOR returned the SpCas9-compatible guides within the first exon. The output includes specificity scores, several predicted efficiency scores and predicted off-target sites.






Figure 3.4: CRISPOR candidate guides for the first exon of OAS2. The table shows guide position, sequence, specificity scores, predicted efficiency scores and off-target information.

3.6 Selected guide RNAs
Two guides were selected by considering predicted efficiency and specificity together. The first-exon sequence and an NGG PAM were required for both. We favoured candidates without reported off-targets at zero, one or two protospacer mismatches and then compared specificity and efficiency scores. Their main values are shown in Table 3.2.

gRNA 1 (200/fw, called 200forw in Task 3) had the higher MIT specificity score (97) and higher Doench 2016 and Moreno-Mateos scores (64 and 48). gRNA 2 (248/fw, or 248forw) had the higher RuleSet3 score (89). Both had a CFD specificity score of 96. We retained gRNA 1 for its stronger MIT score and gRNA 2 as an alternative supported by RuleSet3. The efficiency models disagree, so there is no single guide that is best under every displayed score.
CRISPOR reported 52 possible off-target sites for each guide. For gRNA 1, the distribution was 0-0-0-4-48 for sites with 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 mismatches; for gRNA 2 it was 0-0-0-5-47. Neither has a reported perfect, one-mismatch or two-mismatch off-target in this search. gRNA 1 has one fewer three-mismatch site. As discussed in Lecture 6, counts alone are insufficient because mismatch position also affects recognition; the CFD model additionally accounts for mismatch type (Haeussler et al. 2016).
The displayed alternatives also support the choice. Compared with 166/rev, 200/fw has higher MIT and CFD specificity (97 versus 90 and 96 versus 92) and fewer reported off-targets (52 versus 79). The 150/rev candidate is marked “Inefficient” and has lower Doench 2016 and RuleSet3 values than 248/fw (31 versus 55 and -77 versus 89). These comparisons support retaining the selected pair for Task 3.
These scores are predictions, not measured success rates. Values should be compared within the same scoring model rather than averaged across models. CRISPOR’s cleavage-based predictions do not directly measure CRISPRi repression. Both guides therefore remain candidates that require individual sequence checks and experimental validation.

title: 3  Task 2: gRNA design for OAS2
text:
3.7 Preparation for Task 3
The selected guides and their off-target information are carried forward to Task 3. The reference-genome design does not confirm that each individual’s target and PAM are unchanged. OAS2 is on chromosome 12, whereas the supplied variant subsets cover chromosomes 1 and 2. Task 3 can therefore reassess off-targets on those chromosomes but cannot confirm OAS2 target availability from those files.
crumbs: 3  Task 2: gRNA design for OAS2

title: 3  Task 2: gRNA design for OAS2
text:
3.8 Task 2 conclusion
OAS2 was selected from the six consensus genes because both expression methods support upregulation and the gene has a documented antiviral role. CRISPRi was chosen under the project’s expression-restoration hypothesis. The 267 bp first exon of ENST00000392583.7 was analysed with GRCh38/hg38 and SpCas9-NGG settings. 200/fw was retained for its stronger MIT specificity and 248/fw as a second candidate with a higher RuleSet3 prediction. Their suitability in individual genomes is assessed within the available data in Task 3.

title: 4  Task 3: Impact of Human Genetic Variation on CRISPR Guide Performance
text:
4.1 Objective
In Task 2, two CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) guides, 200forw and 248forw, were selected for the first exon of OAS2 using CRISPOR predictions (Haeussler et al. 2016). Human genetic variation may change an intended target or a predicted off-target site. Task 3 asks whether each genome still contains a matching target and PAM, and whether off-target recognition changes. The chromosome 1/2 analysis checks predicted off-target sites. A separate chromosome 12 analysis checks both intended OAS2 targets in the same seven individuals.
crumbs: 4  Task 3: Impact of Human Genetic Variation on CRISPR Guide Performance

title: 4  Task 3: Impact of Human Genetic Variation on CRISPR Guide Performance
text:
4.2 Approach
The CRISPOR off-target prediction table generated in Task 2 was originally imported into a Python Jupyter Notebook and filtered to include only the selected OAS2 guides (200forw and 248forw). Predicted off-target coordinates, guide sequences, mismatch counts and off-target scores were extracted for further analysis. Reusing these predictions provided a direct way to refine the guide selection from Task 2, while keeping the same candidate guides.
Variant information came from the chromosome 1 and chromosome 2 VCF files used in the original analysis. They contain genotypes for HG00142, HG00178, HG00237, HG01521, HG03129, NA19175 and NA19462. A VCF records the reference and alternate alleles, positions and individual genotypes (Danecek et al. 2011). Variant positions were compared with reference-predicted off-target intervals on these two chromosomes. The full recognition region includes the protospacer and PAM, since a variant in either may matter. Predicted off-target sites on other chromosomes and new variant-created sites were not searched.
For the single overlapping SNP, the original notebook recorded the reference and alternate off-target sequences. This R analysis separates each 23-base sequence into the 20-base protospacer matched by the guide and the 3-base PAM. Mismatches are counted only in the protospacer. This follows the target structure discussed in Lecture 6: a 20-base sequence next to a canonical NGG PAM. Mismatch position and type also matter, so the count alone cannot quantify off-target activity (Haeussler et al. 2016).
The genotype was used to distinguish reference homozygotes, heterozygotes and alternate homozygotes. In the VCF, 0 denotes the reference allele, 1 the first alternate allele, and | indicates phased alleles (Danecek et al. 2011). The original CRISPOR MIT and CFD scores were not recalculated and are not presented as scores for the alternate sequence.
The intended targets were checked separately in chromosome 12 data using a Jupyter Notebook in VS Code. The input was ALL.chr12.shapeit2_integrated_snvindels_v2a_27022019.GRCh38.phased.vcf from the IGSR 20190312_biallelic_SNV_and_INDEL release. Its header identifies GRCh38. The notebook read the full file and retained records overlapping the two 23-base target-plus-PAM regions: chr12:112978698–112978720 for 200forw and chr12:112978746–112978768 for 248forw. Coordinates are 1-based and inclusive, and both sequences are on the forward strand.
The Task 2 target sequences were checked against the saved Ensembl GRCh38 first-exon sequence. For each overlapping record, the VCF REF allele was checked against this reference. SNP alleles were then applied to each chromosome copy using the seven individuals’ genotypes. The notebook counted 20-base protospacer mismatches and checked the PAM separately. The code flags missing calls, alternate indels and uncertain phase for review. The saved results record that sequence coverage was not checked.
Data provenance and scope. The original chromosome 1/2 overlap analysis and the new chromosome 12 target check were performed in Python. This R chapter uses the original carrier CSV and sequence/genotype snapshot, together with the new chromosome 12 exports, to regenerate the tables. It recalculates sequence differences and genotype interpretation, but does not rerun either raw VCF scan during rendering. The chromosome 12 notebook records its reference checks, input header, results and actual software versions. The Reproducibility chapter explains how to repeat that scan. For the original chromosome 1/2 scan, agreement between assemblies, coordinates, strand and REF alleles must still be checked from its raw inputs.
crumbs: 4  Task 3: Impact of Human Genetic Variation on CRISPR Guide Performance

title: 4  Task 3: Impact of Human Genetic Variation on CRISPR Guide Performance
text:
4.3 Findings

Guide Availability in Individual Genomes
The chromosome 12 check found no overlapping VCF record for 200forw and four overlapping records for 248forw. At all four 248forw sites, every selected individual has the reference genotype 0|0. Therefore, none of the seven individuals carries a called alternate allele at these sites. The four records describe sites that vary in the wider dataset, rather than four changes in the selected individuals.
Both reconstructed copies match the corresponding 20-base guide sequence and retain TGG in all seven individuals: zero protospacer mismatches and two matching copies per person in the supplied calls (Table 4.1). The result is the same for HG00142, HG00178, HG00237, HG01521, HG03129, NA19175 and NA19462.


Show analysis code
chr12 <- read_task3("Task3_chr12_on_target_summary.csv")
chr12_variants <- read_task3("Task3_chr12_on_target_variants.csv")
chr12_reference <- c(
  "200forw" = "TCAGACACTGATCGACGAGATGG",
  "248forw" = "GGAACCCGAACAGTTCCCCCTGG")
stopifnot(nrow(chr12) == length(selected_guides) * length(samples),
          setequal(chr12$Guide, selected_guides),
          setequal(chr12$Sample, samples),
          !anyDuplicated(chr12[c("Guide", "Sample")]),
          all(chr12$End - chr12$Start == 22L))
for (copy in 1:2) {
  sequences <- chr12[[paste0("Copy_", copy, "_sequence")]]
  recalculated <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(chr12)), function(i)
    mm20(chr12_reference[[chr12$Guide[i]]], sequences[i]), integer(1))
  stopifnot(all(recalculated == chr12[[paste0("Mismatches_", copy)]]),
            all(vapply(sequences, pam, character(1)) ==
                chr12[[paste0("PAM_", copy)]]))
}
chr12_gt <- t(vapply(chr12_variants$GT, split_gt, integer(2)))
stopifnot(!anyNA(chr12_gt))
chr12_alt <- rowSums(chr12_gt > 0L) > 0L
chr12_sites <- unique(chr12_variants[c("Guide", "Chromosome", "POS", "REF", "ALT")])
chr12_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(selected_guides, function(g) {
  x <- chr12[chr12$Guide == g, ]
  n_records <- sum(chr12_sites$Guide == g)
  stopifnot(all(x$Overlapping_records == n_records))
  carriers <- unique(chr12_variants$Sample[chr12_variants$Guide == g & chr12_alt])
  copies <- unique(x$Matching_copies_in_called_data)
  data.frame(Guide = g,
    `GRCh38 target + PAM` = paste0("chr12:", x$Start[1], "-", x$End[1]),
    `Overlapping records` = n_records,
    `ALT carriers` = paste0(length(carriers), "/", length(samples)),
    `Matching copies per person` = paste(sort(copies), collapse = ", "),
    check.names = FALSE)
}))

Variants Affecting Predicted Off-Target Sites
Comparison of predicted off-target coordinates with the chromosome 1 and chromosome 2 VCF datasets identified a single variant overlapping a predicted off-target site associated with guide 248forw (Table 4.3). The variant was a G to A substitution at chromosome 1 position 224,887,199. Effect on Off-Target Binding Risk
The G to A substitution changes the PAM of the reported off-target sequence from AGG to AGA (Table 4.5). It does not change the 20-base protospacer: its mismatch count remains 4 before and 4 after the variant. The alternate allele removes the canonical NGG PAM. Under the NGG-based framework used for guide selection, this makes the alternate sequence a less suitable off-target candidate. This is a qualitative prediction; it does not establish zero binding or a measured reduction in activity. Noncanonical PAMs can sometimes support Cas9 activity (Haeussler et al. 2016).
Individual-level analysis showed different effects depending on genotype (Table 4.6). 3 individuals are heterozygous: one haplotype has the altered AGA PAM, while the other retains the reference AGG PAM. NA19462 is homozygous for the alternate allele, so both haplotypes have the altered PAM. Consequently, all four carriers should not be assigned the same whole-individual reduction in risk. Allele copy counts do not imply a proportional change in binding.

title: 4  Task 3: Impact of Human Genetic Variation on CRISPR Guide Performance
text:
4.4 Discussion
The SNP changes one predicted 248forw off-target PAM while leaving the protospacer at four mismatches. For HG00142, HG03129 and NA19175, only one haplotype has the changed PAM; the other retains AGG. For NA19462, both haplotypes have AGA. HG00178, HG00237 and HG01521 retain AGG on both copies. This refines Task 2 by giving a genotype-specific interpretation of one reference-predicted site, rather than assigning the same change to all seven individuals. Human variants can create or remove PAMs and change recognition at intended and unintended sites (Lessard et al. 2017).
The evidence supports keeping both guides as candidates for further assessment. The chromosome 12 check found no called target or PAM change for either guide in any of the seven individuals. No overlapping variant was reported for 200forw in the chromosome 1/2 off-target subset. For 248forw, the SNP does not improve the protospacer match and removes the canonical PAM on ALT haplotypes. This does not establish that either guide is safer overall. Other predicted sites were not assessed, and variants may create sites absent from the reference-based list. Reconstructing individual haplotypes and repeating the search, or using a variant-aware tool, would address that question. Reliable sequence coverage across the chromosome 12 targets is still needed before confirming complete guide availability.
This project uses CRISPRi, which regulates transcription using nuclease-deactivated Cas9 rather than cutting DNA (Jensen et al. 2021). Therefore, these results concern potential off-target recognition and unintended gene regulation. CRISPOR cleavage-based scores do not directly measure CRISPRi repression. Experimental validation would be needed to confirm the functional effect of the PAM change.
crumbs: 4  Task 3: Impact of Human Genetic Variation on CRISPR Guide Performance

title: 4  Task 3: Impact of Human Genetic Variation on CRISPR Guide Performance
text:
4.5 Conclusion
Analysis of the supplied results identified one SNP overlapping a reference-predicted off-target site for guide 248forw in four of seven individuals. The variant changes the PAM from AGG to AGA while leaving the protospacer mismatch count at four. Three carriers are heterozygous and retain one reference haplotype; NA19462 is homozygous for the alternate allele. No overlapping variant was reported for guide 200forw in the chromosome 1/2 subset. The chromosome 12 check found no target or PAM change in the supplied calls for either guide in any of the seven individuals. Complete guide availability remains conditional because sequence coverage was not checked. The findings support individual genotype checks, while a wider analysis is needed to assess guide suitability.
The Reproducibility chapter documents the input files, data access, reproduction workflow and software information. Sources cited here are included in the final References.

title: 5  Summary
text:
5.1 Findings across the three tasks
The project connects differential-expression analysis, guide design and individual variant assessment. Task 1 found 68 significant genes with DESeq2 and 7 with edgeR. Six genes were significant in both tools with the same direction of change: OAS2, GPRASP1, AC026801.2, IFI27, SERPINB2 and CXCL11. Five were upregulated and SERPINB2 was downregulated. The intersection favours agreement between methods, but may leave out real changes detected by only one tool.
Task 2 selected OAS2 because both methods supported increased expression and it has a documented antiviral role. Its log2 fold changes were 9.90 and 10.30, although low mock counts and two donors limit the interpretation of these large values. CRISPRi was chosen under the project’s working hypothesis; the analysis does not show that reducing OAS2 would improve recovery.
CRISPOR identified 200forw and 248forw as candidates in the first exon. Their MIT specificity scores were 97 and 89, and both had a CFD specificity score of 96. Each had 52 reported off-targets, with none at zero, one or two mismatches in that search. 200forw had stronger MIT specificity, while 248forw had the higher RuleSet3 prediction. Neither prediction establishes experimental CRISPRi activity.
Task 3 refines the reference-based assessment using reported variant and genotype information for seven individuals. One G>A variant at chr1:224,887,199 overlaps a predicted off-target site for 248forw. The variant changes the PAM from AGG to AGA, while the 20-base protospacer remains unchanged at four mismatches. This alters the sequence’s suitability under the canonical NGG-PAM framework; it does not provide a measured change in off-target activity.
The effect differs between individuals. HG00142, HG03129 and NA19175 are heterozygous and retain the reference PAM on one haplotype. NA19462 is homozygous for the alternate allele and has the changed PAM on both haplotypes. Thus, one variant is present in four individuals, with different allele-level implications. No overlapping variant was reported for 200forw in the chromosome 1/2 subset assessed.
The intended OAS2 targets were also checked using chromosome 12 data. No overlapping VCF record was found for 200forw, while four were found for 248forw. All seven individuals had the reference genotype 0|0 at all four sites. Both local copies reconstructed from the supplied calls had zero protospacer mismatches and retained TGG for both guides in all seven individuals. These results describe the supplied variant calls; sequence coverage was not checked.

title: 5  Summary
text:
5.2 Implications for guide selection
The guides selected in Task 2 remain candidates for further evaluation. The variant finding illustrates why an individual genome can differ from the reference-based prediction (Lessard et al. 2017). It is not sufficient to rank one guide as safer overall or to confirm either guide for every individual.
The chromosome 12 check found no called change in either intended target or PAM for the seven individuals. Reliable sequence coverage across those regions still needs to be confirmed. The off-target comparison also cannot identify new sites created by variants outside the original CRISPOR list. A wider variant-aware search is needed to address this limitation.
The interpretation also needs to match the proposed CRISPRi system. CRISPRi regulates transcription rather than cutting DNA (Jensen et al. 2021). Cleavage-based prediction scores therefore support candidate assessment but do not directly establish the extent of off-target gene regulation.

title: 5  Summary
text:
5.3 Overall conclusion
Task 1 identified six consensus candidates, and Task 2 selected two OAS2 guides for further evaluation. Task 3 identified a genotype-dependent PAM change at one predicted 248forw off-target site. The chromosome 12 check found no target or PAM change in the supplied calls for either guide in any of the seven individuals. Checking sequence coverage and searching for variant-created off-targets would strengthen individual guide assessment. Experimental work would still be needed to test guide activity and biological effects.

title: 6  Reproducibility
text:
6.1 Project files and data access
The report is organised as a Quarto book. The chapter source files, _quarto.yml, references.bib, the data and figures folders, and renv.lock should be kept together in the Final Report project folder. The R chapters use relative paths so that they can be moved to another computer without retaining a personal Windows directory.
The group shares the project through its GitHub repository. The Final Report/data folder is the shared location for report data. For reproduction, retain the repository copy used for the report, or record its commit identifier, because the contents of the main branch can change.
The following files are used by the R chapters or record the evidence for the chromosome 12 target check.
The original chromosome 1 and chromosome 2 VCF inputs are stored in the group’s Project/00_data/vcf_data folder. The filenames used in the original notebook are sampled_chr1.vcf and sampled_chr2.vcf. These files are the course-provided subset of 1000 Genomes variant data for the same seven individuals. They are separate from the small CSV exports used to render the revised Task 3 chapter.
The chromosome 12 check uses a separate, full-chromosome IGSR input: ALL.chr12.shapeit2_integrated_snvindels_v2a_27022019.GRCh38.phased.vcf. The compressed file is available from the IGSR 20190312_biallelic_SNV_and_INDEL release. The completed run used the unpacked VCF, 35,466,361,650 bytes, and selected the same seven sample IDs. Its header records GRCh38. This input has a different scope from the course-provided chromosome 1/2 subsets; the chromosome 12 results concern the two intended target regions only.

title: 6  Reproducibility
text:
6.3 Reproduction workflow
To reproduce the report, obtain the project source files and data, retain their folder structure, and open Final Report.Rproj in RStudio. Use a fresh R session and restore the project dependencies recorded in renv.lock. Render the complete book in HTML format from the project folder. The book configuration lists the task chapters in analysis order and disables both execution caching and frozen results.
The stages have the following dependencies:

Task 1 reads the RNA-seq count matrix, performs the DESeq2 and edgeR analyses, and writes the consensus results to data/consensus_table.rds.
Task 2 reads those consensus results and documents the choice of OAS2, the first-exon sequence, CRISPOR settings and selected guides. Guide design is an external CRISPOR step. Repeating it requires the input sequence and settings reported in Task 2 and the corresponding saved tool exports.
Task 3 reads the two original off-target CSV inputs and the two chromosome 12 result CSVs. It recalculates the sequence comparisons and regenerates the off-target genotype tables and chromosome 12 summary tables.

Rendering the book reproduces its enabled R calculations and tables from the saved inputs. The external CRISPOR analysis and both Python VCF scans are separate steps. Repeating the original chromosome 1/2 scan requires the original notebook code, sampled_chr1.vcf, sampled_chr2.vcf and the CRISPOR off-target export offtargetsguide.txt. The assembly, coordinate convention and strand orientation must agree between those inputs. The saved Task 3 CSVs allow the reported sequence and genotype interpretation to be reproduced, but do not by themselves repeat the original search for overlapping variants.
To repeat the chromosome 12 check:

Open Task3_chr12_on_target.ipynb in VS Code or Jupyter and select the Python kernel. The recorded run used Python 3.13.0 and pandas 2.3.3.
Obtain and unpack the chromosome 12 VCF above. In the first notebook cell, set VCF_PATH to the location of this file on your computer. The saved notebook contains the path used for the completed run; change that path for another computer. Keep the seven sample IDs and both target coordinates unchanged.
Place a copy of data/Task3_chr12_reference_exon.fasta in the chr12_results folder printed by the first notebook cell to reuse the recorded reference. If it is absent, the reference-check cell downloads the exon sequence using the Ensembl URL recorded in the environment JSON. The target regions are chr12:112978698–112978720 and chr12:112978746–112978768, with 1-based inclusive coordinates on the forward strand.
Restart the kernel and run all cells in order. The notebook checks the reference targets, confirms the VCF assembly and sample IDs, scans overlapping records, checks REF alleles, reconstructs both local copies and exports five result files. Continue to export only after the scan finishes without errors. The complete VCF was read for the recorded run.
Copy the five exported Task3_chr12_* files from chr12_results into Final Report/data, keeping their filenames. Retain the executed notebook beside the QMD chapters as Task3_chr12_on_target.ipynb. Then render the book to regenerate the chromosome 12 tables from the new exports.

The recorded check returned zero overlapping records for 200forw and four for 248forw. All seven individuals have 0|0 at all four sites. The summary therefore contains 14 guide–individual rows, each with zero protospacer mismatches, TGG on both copies and two matching copies in the supplied calls. The variants export has 28 rows because it lists four sites for seven individuals. These counts are checks on the recorded output, not required results for a different VCF dataset.
The notebook reconstructs SNP alleles and flags alternate indels, complex calls, missing genotypes and uncertain phase for review. The saved environment records coverage_checked: false. Thus, a count of two matching copies describes the supplied calls; absence of a variant record is not proof of reliable sequence coverage. A fresh notebook run repeats the raw chromosome 12 scan, while rendering alone reads its exports.
